children: By Emma Tucker
From My Desk:

When the U.S. launched its campaign against Iran six months ago, Pete Hegseth promised a quick, decisive blow that would avoid a long entanglement. Now, our reporting shows the Pentagon is quietly extending troop deployments, signaling the conflict could drag well into 2027. It's part of an open-ended military strategy designed to give President Trump options in the war. But the move is putting a significant strain on servicemembers and their families — and creating a maintenance backlog that could take years to unwind. The Pentagon's all-in approach comes as Trump sends mixed signals on what comes next.
Today's Headlines
Ted Cruz isn't hiding his presidential ambitions — and he is taking some digs at presumptive front-runner JD Vance along the way.
Steve Bannon has made a career out of clashing with far-left politicians. But these days, Trump's former chief strategist has found a common cause with them: opposition to the AI boom.
Trump's plan to lower gas prices by tapping Venezuelan oil faces steep uncertainties, and it's unclear it would provide relief to Americans at the pump.
Anna Wintour's quest to reclaim British designer John Galliano's legacy was thwarted by politicians and donors.
The NBA delivered one of the harshest penalties in league history to the Los Angeles Clippers and owner Steve Ballmer, for what it called a "flagrant violation" of its salary-cap rules.
Live From The Markets
The hunt for assets insulated from the AI boom is leading investors to more analog pursuits: sports teams, iconic real estate and even children's toys.
Investors in Boeing face another headwind, as the plane maker uncovered additional liabilities beyond what it initially recognized after it closed its biggest deal in years, writes Jonathan Weil.
Under his "Donroe" doctrine, Trump no longer treats Venezuela as sovereign. Canada fears the same treatment, writes Greg Ip.
Read It Here First
Ford's $30,000 EV truck has an ambitious goal.

Ford is aiming to sell more than 100,000 of its new electric trucks in its first year of production, according to people familiar with the matter. The truck, called the Ford Fathom, starts at around $30,000 and goes on sale next year. Executives have said the truck will feature technology designed to compete with Tesla and upstart Chinese automakers, with a price tag similar to mainstream sedans and SUVs. If it meets Ford's targets, Fathom would instantly become one of the top-selling EVs in the U.S., reports Ryan Felton.
China's warships are cruising too close for comfort off Japan's shores.

Japan is facing what officials describe as the most severe security environment since World War II. China is flexing its growing military might, pressing its maritime claims across eastern Asia and pushing deeper into the Western Pacific, where the U.S. has held sway for years. Japanese surveillance has recorded Chinese destroyers passing through the strait near Amami-Oshima at least 10 times this year. That follows zero such transits in 2025 and is on pace to exceed the 15 recorded in 2024. Deepening alliances among Japan's near neighbors — China, North Korea and Russia — have raised questions about the nation's security, as well as that of vital sea lanes that connect its economy to the U.S. and beyond, report Jason Douglas and Junko Fukutome.
See The Story
There are four forces pressuring bonds. War is No. 1.

Worries about runaway government spending. A new Federal Reserve chairman. The huge surge in bond issuance to fund the artificial-intelligence build-out. There are many forces pushing Treasury yields higher. But the main driver of the recent run-up: inflation. While a confluence of factors have powered the global bond slide that carried yields to multiyear highs around the world, a look inside market shifts suggests the key factor in the U.S. remains the sharp climb in energy prices driven by the war in Iran.
Happening Today
Earnings: Victoria's Secret, Campbell's, Lululemon Athletica, Smith & Wesson
Number Of The Day:

The rough share of Common App partner colleges now using "direct admissions" to accept students who didn't even fill out an application. Facing a dwindling pipeline of 18-year-olds, schools are increasingly agreeing to admit applicants based on a handful of criteria like high school transcripts — a free process that skips required essays, questions about extracurriculars and standardized tests.
And Finally...
Nothing makes humans happier right now than watching robots fail.

Feeling a little terrified about how quickly technology seems to be sidelining humanity? Try watching a robot sprint straight into a wall. It's hilarious. In recent videos showing machines on two legs running track in Beijing, some succeeded in breaking Usain Bolt's 100-meter record. And some slammed full tilt into a barrier, collapsing and reeling like drunks. More than one flopped backward in a cartoonish froth of sparks. It's content that delivers pure physical comedy, guilt-free schadenfreude and a reassuring feeling of superiority.
